_comment: Shahnama of Firdausi, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. IV: Twelve Rukhs duels, Piran's death, Kai Khusrau's ascension. Paraphrase passages with notes.

title.en: Bizhan Slays Human on the Waterless Waste

region.zh: 卡納巴德附近荒漠（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. IV, Twelve Rukhs secs. 14-15

summary.en: Human challenges Bizhan and names the scene: wilt thou contend with me upon Mount Kanabad, or make the scene Raibad, and far from aid on either side? They agreed: whichever shall survive shall spare the fallen man's interpreter to bear his king the news. They fought from morning till the shadows lengthened with bows, spears, swords, maces, and wrestling, till by consent they hastened to a pool, and Bizhan prayed: if thou perceivest justice in my cause, the strength which I possess take not away. Though Human was mightier, all prowess is but defect in him whose sun is set: Bizhan bent that mighty Camel, raised him aloft, flung him to the ground, drew forth a dagger, swift as wind beheaded him, and donned instead the armour of Human.
summary.zh: 胡曼向比讚叫陣：「在卡納巴德山，還是去兩軍莫及的荒漠決戰？」二人約定：倖存者須放走敗者的通譯以報信。自晨戰至日斜——弓、矛、劍、錘、角力——同赴泉邊；比讚祈禱：「若我師出有名，請勿奪我之力。」胡曼雖勇，然「其日已落，勇武皆成缺陷」——比讚如豹出爪，彎折駱駝般的巨軀、高舉過頂、擲落於地，拔匕首如風斬其首，然後披上胡曼的鎧甲。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the duel echoes the Rustam-Sohrab wrestling. No living community restriction.

passages.text: When morning breathed above the mountain-tops Human equipped himself, and told Piran: I challenged Bizhan, the son of Giv, and spent the night preparing. Human replied: to-day Giv's heart shall break for his bold son. Wilt thou contend with me upon Mount Kanabad, or make the scene Raibad, and far from aid on either side? They left Mount Kanabad, rode toward the waste, and reached a desert-spot where they beheld no footprints left by man, where vultures flew not, and lions trod not, far from host and help. There they agreed: whichever shall survive shall spare the fallen man's interpreter to bear his king the news of what befell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Twelve Rukhs sec. 14 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: They strained their bows until the notches touched, discharged their poplar arrows tipped with steel, then took their spears, and wheeled to left and right; they took their maces, having done with swords, and passed all measure in their combating; thereafter they essayed each other's strength, and neither of them had the mastery. Bizhan, when he had drunk, arose in anguish, all shaking like a willow in a gale, and, in his heart despairing of sweet life, called upon God: if thou perceivest justice in my cause, both in my challenge and my purposes, the strength which I possess take not away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Twelve Rukhs sec. 14 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Human, distressed and raven-black with pain, advanced. All wounded as they were both came like pards to fight again, and first one, then the other, touched the ground. For, though Human was mightier, all prowess is but defect in him whose sun is set. Bizhan put forth his hands like leopard's claws: his left hand gripped his foeman's neck, the right his foeman's thigh, he bent that mighty Camel, raised him aloft, and flung him to the ground; then holding down Human, and drawing forth a dagger, swift as wind beheaded him, and flung away his carcase like a dragon's.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Twelve Rukhs sec. 15 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Bizhan surveyed that elephantine form, fall'n like a stately cypress in a meadow, with great amazement, turned away, looked up to Him who ruleth o'er the world and said: I have no portion in this doughty deed, not having pluck to fight an elephant, yet have cut off Human's head in revenge for Siyawush, and my sire's seventy brothers. Fearing lest the Turkman multitude should come forth to battle while he was not prepared to fight alone, he put from him the mail of Siyawush and donned instead the armour of Human, then mounted on the elephantine steed and took in hand the banner of that prince.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Twelve Rukhs sec. 15 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Gudarz Shoots Piran's Steed; the Wise Man Falls
title.zh: 古達爾茲射殺皮蘭坐騎

region.en: Field of the Eleven Rukhs (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 十一勇士戰場（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. IV, Twelve Rukhs secs. 29-39

summary.en: Gudarz and Piran arrange a battle of Eleven Rukhs; the paired champions fight one by one, and when the ninth hour of the day had passed there was no Turkman left on that broad plain. Disaster came upon Piran from God; against that will he had no remedy, for the will that made his steed fail under him. Gudarz chose out a poplar arrow that would pierce iron, shot it mightily, and pierced the armour of his foeman's steed, which shivered, gasped, and fell; Piran fell under, his right hand was broken, and he fled from Gudarz toward the hill: born was I in the world for death. Gudarz wept bitterly and shouted: ask quarter for thy life that I may bear thee still living to the Shah — and Piran answers: God forbid! To beg my life were heaviness indeed.
summary.zh: 古達爾茲與皮蘭約定「十一勇士之戰」，兩軍名將逐一配對搏殺；日過九時，圖蘭無一騎存留。天災降於皮蘭——「使他的坐騎失蹄的正是天意」——古達爾茲選一支能穿鐵的白楊箭，大力射出，穿透敵騎甲胄；馬嘶而斃，皮蘭墜地，右手折斷，蹣跚奔向山丘：「人生在世本為一死。」老將含淚高呼：「求饒吧，我帶你去見王！」答曰：「神明在上——乞命之辱，我寧死不受！」

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; Piran, Turan's wise elder, dies a soldier's death. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Whenas the ninth hour of the day had passed there was no Turkman left on that broad plain: their lives had been dissevered by the sword. Thou wouldst have said: the world is pitiless! Whenas the Turkmans in those luckless combats had struggled fruitlessly Piran descried none of his champions left upon the field; the leaders of Iran and of Turan advanced together for their grim revenge, grief in their hearts and vengeance in their heads.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Twelve Rukhs secs. 26-39 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Those cavaliers tried every kind of sleight with sword and brand, with lasso and with mace, but Heaven's purposes were brought to pass; disaster came upon Piran from God; against that will he had no remedy, the will that made his steed fail under him. Piran saw well enough how matters stood, and knew that God had caused that change of fortune, yet he acquitted him right manfully, and strove against the purposes of fate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Twelve Rukhs sec. 39 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The two chiefs of the host, those shrewd old men, then took their bows and arrows in their hands. Gudarz chose out a poplar arrow, one that would pierce iron, shot it mightily, and pierced the armour of his foeman's steed, which shivered, gasped, and fell. Piran fell under; his steed rolled o'er him; his right hand was broken. He struggled out and rose upon his feet. Though knowing well that his last hour had come, and that he could not scape from that dark day, yet fled he from Gudarz toward the hill.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Twelve Rukhs sec. 39 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: O famous paladin! what aileth thee that thou dost foot it thus like game before me? shouted Gudarz, weeping bitterly; ask quarter for thy life that I may bear thee still living to the Shah; that conquering one will pardon thee because, like me, thou art a hoary paladin. Now God forbid! Piran replied: God grant that no such ill befall my latter end and I survive. To beg my life were heaviness indeed! Born was I in the world for death, and I thus fighting put my neck within thy power.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Twelve Rukhs sec. 39 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Khusrau Builds Piran a Charnel and Executes Gurwi
title.zh: 霍斯勞葬皮蘭而誅吉爾維

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. IV, Twelve Rukhs sec. 47

summary.en: The Shah surveyed the slain and, when he saw the Turkman general, shed tears of sorrow, remembering Piran's good offices: thou hast been troubled for me all my life; this man deplored the blood of Siyawush, and in that matter gave offence to none; but Ahriman seduced his heart and turned his rede to other ends. The mountain was Piran's grave, and Khusrau in his affection had a charnel built, and raised its summit to the turning sky; within it there were set up princes' thrones, and they placed the Turkman paladins thereon with belted waists and crowns upon their heads. Then Khusrau looked upon Gurwi, the son of Zira, cursing him as he deserved, and bade disjoint Gurwi with cords and fling into a stream, first cutting off the head.
summary.zh: 王巡視屍場，見圖蘭主帥而落淚，追念皮蘭平生的恩義：「他一生為我憂勞；他憐惜西亞瓦什之血，未曾開罪於人；只是阿赫里曼蠱惑其心。」皮蘭葬於山中，霍斯勞因情築陵，陵頂直指蒼穹，內設君王寶座，讓圖蘭勇士束腰戴冠端坐其上。隨後王直面弑西亞瓦什的兇手吉爾維，咒其罪愆，先斬其首，再以繩拆解其身投入河中。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; royal mourning and justice. No living community restriction.

passages.text: The Shah then surveyed the slain and, when he saw the Turkman general, shed tears of sorrow, remembering Piran's good offices; his heart burned so that thou hadst said: it flameth! Ill fortune is a Dragon grim and snareth great lions with its breath, he made oration o'er that chieftain's death: thou hast been troubled for me all my life, and hast for my sake laboured strenuously. This man deplored the blood of Siyawush, and in that matter gave offence to none; but Ahriman seduced his heart and turned his rede to other ends.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Twelve Rukhs sec. 47 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He ordered that the body should be washed with musk, pure camphor, and rose-water mixed with spices, and embalmed with musk and camphor, and clad it stainless with brocade of Rum. The mountain was Piran's grave, and Khusrau in his affection had a charnel built, and raised its summit to the turning sky. Within it there were set up princes' thrones, such as befitted men of high degree, and they placed the Turkman paladins thereon with belted waists and crowns upon their heads.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Twelve Rukhs sec. 47 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Khusrau then looked upon Gurwi, the son of Zira, cursing him as he deserved, looked on that loathly face wherefrom the hair hung down like divs', and said: O God! Thou knowest the manifest and hidden. Of a truth Kaus had done amiss and grieved the Maker in that He raised up such a div as this 'gainst Siyawush. I wot not why Gurwi should hate that faultless one, but by His might who ruleth all and giveth good, I will have vengeance on Afrasiyab for Siyawush and soon. He bade disjoint Gurwi with cords and fling into a stream, first cutting off, as 'twere a sheep's, the head: so must I treat Afrasiyab, he said.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Twelve Rukhs sec. 47 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Kai Khusrau Walks into the Mountain and Vanishes

region.zh: 伊朗境外群山（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. IV, Kai Khusrau secs. 62-63

summary.en: Khusrau, his vengeance wrought, makes Luhrasp Shah and leads seven chiefs toward the mountains: my day hath passed. A hundred thousand Iranians follow weeping; three turn back at his command — Zal, Rustam, and old Gudarz — but Tus, Giv, Fariburz, Bizhan, and Gustaham press on. At a spring by night the Shah bathes and recites the Zandavasta: farewell for ever! when the sky shall bring the sun again ye shall not look on me henceforth save in your dreams. When the sun rose the Shah had disappeared; then there came up storm and cloud, the sky became as 'twere a lion's hide, and when the snow had hoisted sail upon the earth the lances of the nobles disappeared — under it they struggled for a while, and at the last strength failed them and they yielded up sweet life.
summary.zh: 大仇已報，霍斯勞立盧赫拉斯普為王，攜七位名將入山：「我的日子已滿。」十萬伊朗人含淚相隨；扎勒、魯斯塔姆、古達爾茲三人奉命折返，圖斯、吉夫、法里布爾茲、比讚與古斯塔哈姆執意前行。泉畔之夜，王沐浴誦經：「永別了！明日太陽重升，你們只能在夢中見我。」日出之時，王已無蹤；隨即風雪驟起、天幕如獅皮，長矛沉入雪海——五壮士掙扎片刻，氣絕於雪底。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the vanished-king motif (cf. Arthur in Celtic tradition). No living community restriction.

passages.text: Khusrau commanded that Luhrasp should come, and said to him: my day hath passed. Go thou, maintain the usage of the royal throne, and in the world sow but the seed of good. From Iran went chieftains with the Shah, great, shrewd, and valiant, as Zal and Rustam, as Gudarz and Giv, the brave Bizhan and gallant Gustaham; the seventh was Fariburz, son of Kaus, the eighth famed Tus. The host marched troop on troop till from the waste they reached a mountain-top, while every archimage said privily: none in the world e'er told of such a case!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Khusrau sec. 62 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: A multitude collected from all parts, and five score thousand of the Iranians, both men and women, went before the Shah in grief; the mount was full of wails and cries, and e'en the flints were moved. Quit not Iran nor give this ancient world a youthful Shah, the people said. Yon desert none may pass who hath not Grace and lofty stature, answered the king; three proud warriors attended to the bidding and turned back — Zal, Rustam, and the old Gudarz — but Tus and Giv and Fariburz, Bizhan, and gallant Gustaham would not return.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Khusrau sec. 62 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: At length a spring was seen upon the way, and thither went the aspiring Kai Khusrau. Here let us make our sojourn for the night, said the Shah, and talk at large together of the past, for henceforth nobody will see me more. What time the radiant sun shall raise its flag, then is the time when I shall pass away, and haply with Suriish for company. As night advanced the famous Kaian went before his God, bathed, head and body, in the limpid stream, reciting to himself the Zandavasta, and thus addressed those famous men of lore: farewell for ever! when the sky shall bring the sun again ye shall not look on me henceforth save in your dreams.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Khusrau sec. 62 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The chieftains' heads were heavy at the news, and when the sun rose o'er the hills the Shah had disappeared. They roamed thence seeking him and saw no trace of Kai Khusrau; meanwhile there came up storm and cloud, the sky became as 'twere a lion's hide, and when the snow had hoisted sail upon the earth the lances of the nobles disappeared! They tarried in the snow, and under it they struggled for a while, and made a hollow space, but at the last strength failed them and they yielded up sweet life. Gudarz, son of Kishwad, shed tears, plucked out his hair, and tore his cheeks: none e'er saw such ills as come upon me from the offspring of Kaus!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kai Khusrau sec. 63 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
